title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
edition: First published: The New England Magazine, Jan 1892

sections.authorBiography: Charlotte Perkins Gilman was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on 3 July 1860, a relative of the Beecher family (Harriet Beecher Stowe was her great-aunt). After the birth of her daughter in 1885 she suffered severe depression and in 1887 was treated by the neurologist S. Weir Mitchell with his "rest cure," which forbade intellectual work; she later said it brought her near breakdown. She separated from her husband, moved to California and became a lecturer and writer on women's economic independence (Women and Economics, 1898) and author of the utopian story Herland (1915). Facing incurable cancer, she ended her life on 17 August 1935.
sections.historicalContext: In the nineteenth century, women with depression or "nervous" illness were often prescribed the "rest cure" of the neurologist S. Weir Mitchell: isolation, bed rest, overfeeding and a ban on intellectual work. Gilman underwent a version of it after the birth of her daughter in 1885. Married women had few legal rights, and doctors (usually men) had great authority over their patients.

publicationAndReception.publication: First published in The New England Magazine in January 1892. Gilman later said the editor of The Atlantic, Horace Scudder, rejected it, writing that he could not forgive himself if he made others as miserable as he had made himself.
publicationAndReception.then: Many readers read it as a horror story about madness; a Boston doctor protested that it could drive readers insane.
publicationAndReception.now: A foundational feminist text, rediscovered in the 1970s (the Feminist Press reissued it in 1973), and a classic of psychological horror and the unreliable narrator.

sections.overview: A young mother, taken by her physician husband John to a rented country house for a "rest cure," keeps a secret journal. She is forbidden to write and confined to a former nursery with hideous yellow wallpaper.
sections.whyItMatters: The story helped change how people thought about depression and women's autonomy, and it remains a powerful study of how silencing someone harms them.

spoilerOverview.text: She becomes convinced a woman is trapped behind the wallpaper's pattern, and in the end she tears it off, identifies with the trapped woman, and creeps around the room as her husband faints.

passage.quote: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Yellow Wallpaper.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Yellow Wallpaper: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (women and medical authority, confinement and madness, voice and silence) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Yellow Wallpaper teaches about women and medical authority. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Charlotte Perkins Gilman develops women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Charlotte Perkins Gilman develops women and medical authority across The Yellow Wallpaper. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Yellow Wallpaper (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of women and medical authority. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Charlotte Perkins Gilman's choices in The Yellow Wallpaper (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of women and medical authority, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Yellow Wallpaper's treatment of women and medical authority in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on women and medical authority in The Yellow Wallpaper, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
